extraPractice.title: Separate one path, exactly one and at least one
extraPractice.prompt: Four independent trials each succeed with probability \(\frac{1}{5}\). Write S for success and F for failure. Find the probabilities of the particular sequence SFFF, exactly one success, at least one success and at most one success.
extraPractice.hint: Exactly one has four possible success positions. At least one excludes only FFFF; at most one includes both zero successes and exactly one.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[P(\mathrm{SFFF})=\frac{1}{5}\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^3=\frac{64}{625}.\]

  2. Exactly one consists of SFFF, FSFF, FFSF and FFFS. They are disjoint and have equal probabilities under this model:

    \[P(\text{exactly one})=4\left(\frac{64}{625}\right)=\frac{256}{625}.\]
  3. \[P(\text{none})=\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^4=\frac{256}{625},\qquad P(\text{at least one})=1-\frac{256}{625}=\frac{369}{625}.\]
  4. \[P(\text{at most one})=\frac{256}{625}+\frac{256}{625}=\frac{512}{625}.\]

extraPractice.title: Unequal chances give unequal sequence weights
extraPractice.prompt: Three independent checks have pass probabilities \(\frac{2}{5},\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{5}\) in that order. Find the probabilities of all passing, exactly two passing, and at least one passing. Given that exactly two pass, find the probability that the third check passes.
extraPractice.hint: Use a separate product for PPF, PFP and FPP. For the final part, retain only the qualifying paths whose third letter is P.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[P(\mathrm{PPP})=\frac{2}{5}\cdot\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{3}{5}=\frac{3}{25}.\]
  2. \[P(\mathrm{PPF})=\frac{2}{25},\qquad P(\mathrm{PFP})=\frac{3}{25},\qquad P(\mathrm{FPP})=\frac{9}{50}.\]
  3. \[P(\text{exactly two})=\frac{2}{25}+\frac{3}{25}+\frac{9}{50}=\frac{19}{50}.\]
  4. \[P(\text{at least one})=1-\frac{3}{5}\cdot\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{5}=\frac{22}{25}.\]

  5. The required numerator is the combined weight of PFP and FPP:

    \[P(\text{third passes}\mid\text{exactly two})=\frac{\frac{3}{25}+\frac{9}{50}}{\frac{19}{50}}=\frac{15}{19}.\]

    The three possible pass-position patterns are not equally likely.

extraPractice.title: Do not count overlapping runs twice
extraPractice.prompt: A fair coin is tossed independently four times. Find the probability of at least one adjacent HH pair. Separately, find the probability of exactly two heads with those two heads adjacent. A student adds the probabilities of HH in positions \(1,2\), \(2,3\), and \(3,4\), obtaining \(\frac{3}{4}\) for the first question. Is that addition valid?

fields.label: At least one adjacent HH pair

options.no: No: some full sequences satisfy more than one adjacent-pair event.
options.yes: Yes: every pair of tosses is independent of every other pair.
options.three: Yes: there are exactly three possible start positions.

extraPractice.hint: List complete four-letter sequences, or classify them by the position of their first HH pair. Either approach must count each sequence once.
extraPractice.solution:
1. All \(16\) four-letter sequences are equally likely. Those containing HH are HHHH, HHHT, HHTH, HHTT, HTHH, THHH, THHT and TTHH.

  2. \[P(\text{at least one HH})=\frac{8}{16}=\frac{1}{2}.\]

  3. Exactly two heads with adjacency leaves only HHTT, THHT and TTHH:

    \[P(\text{exactly two adjacent heads})=\frac{3}{16}.\]

  4. The proposed three pair-events overlap. For example, HHHH belongs to all three, so adding their probabilities counts it repeatedly. Independent tosses do not make these overlapping run-events disjoint.

extraPractice.title: Distinguish reaching the limit from succeeding there
extraPractice.prompt: Exactly one of eight distinct keys opens a lock. Keys are tried in a uniformly random order without repetition. The procedure stops on success or after the third attempt. Let \(T\) be the number of attempts actually made, and \(W\) the event that the lock opens. Find \(P(W)\), \(P(T=3)\), \(P(W\mid T=3)\) and \(P(T=3\mid W)\).
extraPractice.hint: Imagine the complete random ordering of all eight keys, even though testing may stop earlier. The working key has an equally likely position from one to eight.
extraPractice.solution:
1. The lock opens within the permitted attempts precisely when the working key is in position \(1,2\) or \(3\), so \(P(W)=\frac{3}{8}\).

  2. Three attempts are made whenever the working key is in position \(3\) or later. Thus

    \[P(T=3)=\frac{6}{8}=\frac{3}{4}.\]

  3. Both success and three attempts occur only when the working key is third:

    \[P(W\cap\{T=3\})=\frac{1}{8}.\]
  4. \[P(W\mid T=3)=\frac{\frac{1}{8}}{\frac{6}{8}}=\frac{1}{6},\qquad P(T=3\mid W)=\frac{\frac{1}{8}}{\frac{3}{8}}=\frac{1}{3}.\]

  5. After two failures, six untried keys remain and one works. This also gives the reached third-attempt success chance \(\frac{1}{6}\); it is not the unconditional chance \(\frac{1}{8}\) of succeeding specifically on attempt three.

extraPractice.title: End a contest as soon as somebody wins twice
extraPractice.prompt: In each round A beats B with probability \(\frac{1}{4}\), independently of previous rounds. There are no draws. The contest stops as soon as either player has won two rounds. Find the probability of an A contest win, the probability of three rounds, and the probability of three rounds given an A contest win. Is AABA an additional terminal sequence?

fields.label: Three rounds given an A contest win

options.no: No: the contest already ended at AA.
options.yes: Yes: A wins the final round.
options.draw: Yes: its first two rounds are drawn.

extraPractice.hint: A wins through AA, ABA or BAA. The contest reaches round three exactly when the first two results differ.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[P(\mathrm{AA})=\frac{1}{16},\qquad P(\mathrm{ABA})=P(\mathrm{BAA})=\frac{3}{64}.\]
  2. \[P(\text{A wins})=\frac{1}{16}+\frac{3}{64}+\frac{3}{64}=\frac{5}{32}.\]
  3. \[P(\text{three rounds})=P(\mathrm{AB})+P(\mathrm{BA})=2\cdot\frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{3}{4}=\frac{3}{8}.\]
  4. \[P(\text{three}\mid\text{A wins})=\frac{\frac{3}{64}+\frac{3}{64}}{\frac{5}{32}}=\frac{3}{5}.\]

  5. AABA cannot occur as a terminal record of this procedure. The second A in its prefix AA already ends the contest, so no later letters are recorded.

starters.title: Use the probability attached to the reached history
starters.question: A contest without draws stops when either player A or B has won twice. A wins the first round with probability \(\frac{2}{3}\). In round two, A wins with probability \(\frac{1}{2}\) if A won round one, but with probability \(\frac{3}{4}\) if B won round one. If a third round is reached, A wins it with probability \(\frac{1}{4}\) after either mixed two-round history. Find the probabilities of an A contest win and three rounds. Given an A contest win, find the probability of three rounds and the probability that A won the first round.
starters.hint: The second-round probabilities depend on the first result. Label each reached branch with its own conditional probability, and stop at AA or BB.
starters.solution:
1. \[P(\mathrm{AA})=\frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{3},\qquad P(\mathrm{BB})=\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{12}.\]
  2. \[P(\mathrm{AB})=\frac{1}{3},\qquad P(\mathrm{BA})=\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{3}{4}=\frac{1}{4}.\]

    Only these two mixed histories continue, giving \(P(\text{three rounds})=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{4}=\frac{7}{12}\).

  3. \[P(\mathrm{ABA})=\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{12},\qquad P(\mathrm{BAA})=\frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{16}.\]
  4. \[P(\text{A wins})=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{12}+\frac{1}{16}=\frac{23}{48}.\]
  5. \[P(\text{three}\mid\text{A wins})=\frac{\frac{1}{12}+\frac{1}{16}}{\frac{23}{48}}=\frac{7}{23}.\]

  6. An A contest win with an A first-round win occurs through AA or ABA:

    \[P(\text{first A}\mid\text{A wins})=\frac{\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{12}}{\frac{23}{48}}=\frac{20}{23}.\]

  7. The remaining terminal paths ABB and BAB have probabilities \(\frac{1}{4}\) and \(\frac{3}{16}\). Along with AA, BB, ABA and BAA, all terminal weights sum to one.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: use the correct history-dependent second-round probabilities.
  • 1 mark: obtain both mixed-history weights.
  • 1 mark: calculate the chance of reaching round three.
  • 1 mark: obtain both three-round A-winning weights.
  • 1 mark: add all disjoint A-winning terminal paths.
  • 1 mark: form the correct numerator for three rounds and an A win.
  • 1 mark: divide by the A-win probability.
  • 1 mark: condition the first-round result using AA and ABA.

starters.title: Count colour sequences as disjoint alternatives
starters.question: Three labels are generated independently. Each label is red, green or blue with probabilities \(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{3},\frac{1}{6}\), respectively. Find the probabilities that all three colours appear, that all labels have the same colour, and that exactly two distinct colours appear. Also find the probability of at least one red label, and the probability that all three colours appear given at least one red label.
starters.hint: All three colours appear through the six orders of RGB. Classify the complete sample by the number of distinct colours: one, two or three. These categories are disjoint and exhaustive.
starters.solution:
1. The six orders are RGB, RBG, GRB, GBR, BRG and BGR. Each has probability \(\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{1}{6}=\frac{1}{36}\), so

    \[P(\text{all three colours})=6\left(\frac{1}{36}\right)=\frac{1}{6}.\]
  2. \[P(\text{all same})=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3+\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^3+\left(\frac{1}{6}\right)^3=\frac{27+8+1}{216}=\frac{1}{6}.\]

  3. Exactly two distinct colours means one colour appears twice and another once. It is the remaining category:

    \[P(\text{exactly two distinct colours})=1-\frac{1}{6}-\frac{1}{6}=\frac{2}{3}.\]
  4. \[P(\text{at least one red})=1-\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3=\frac{7}{8}.\]

  5. All three colours necessarily includes red. Therefore the conditional numerator is the all-three probability:

    \[P(\text{all three}\mid\text{at least one red})=\frac{\frac{1}{6}}{\frac{7}{8}}=\frac{4}{21}.\]

    The \(27\) ordered colour strings are not equally likely; only strings containing the same numbers of each colour have equal weights under this fixed-probability model.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: list or account for all six orders containing all three colours.
  • 1 mark: calculate their common path probability and total.
  • 1 mark: form the weighted sum of the three all-same paths.
  • 1 mark: calculate that sum.
  • 1 mark: identify the one/two/three-colour partition.
  • 1 mark: find exactly two distinct colours by subtraction.
  • 1 mark: find the positive conditioning probability using a complement.
  • 1 mark: use containment and divide by that conditioning probability.

revision.body:
Multiply the probabilities on each valid path, then add disjoint alternatives.

Fixed independent trials with a constant success chance

For \(0<p<1\), put \(q=1-p\). In \(n\) fixed trials, let \(X\) count successes. One specified string with \(k\) successes has weight \(p^kq^{n-k}\).

\[P(X=1)=npq^{n-1},\qquad P(X\ge1)=1-q^n.\]

Count every permitted placement. At most one includes zero and one; at least two excludes both. At \(p=0\) or \(p=1\), only all F or all S can occur.

Unequal chances and patterns need their actual path weights

For independent chances \(p_1,p_2,p_3\),

\[P(\mathrm{SFS})=p_1(1-p_2)p_3.\]

Other placements may have different weights. For dependent trials, use each reached branch’s conditional probability. Outgoing labels sum to one.

For adjacency, list full strings once. Overlapping pair-events cannot simply be added.

One working key, no repeats, at most \(r\) attempts

For \(m\) distinct keys in uniform random order, exactly one working key and \(1\le r\le m\),

\[P(\text{success by }r)=\frac{r}{m},\quad P(\text{reach }r)=\frac{m-r+1}{m},\]\[P(\text{success on }r\mid\text{reach }r)=\frac{1}{m-r+1}.\]

Include failure at the limit if possible. Stop on success; removing failed keys changes the next chance.

First to two wins: end every path immediately

Terminal paths: AA, BB, ABA, ABB, BAA, BAB. For independent rounds, A-win chance \(p\), and \(q=1-p\), let \(W\) mean A wins the contest and \(L\) mean three rounds:

\[P(W)=p^2+2p^2q,\qquad P(L)=2pq.\]\[P(L\mid W)=\frac{2q}{1+2q}\qquad(p>0).\]

At \(p=0\), conditioning on an A win is undefined. Changing-history chances need their actual conditional branches.
revision.checks: • Disjoint paths, correct branches, stopping rule and positive conditioning denominator?
revision.examTip: Show each method, retain the required precision and state the complete answer.

orig_9709_s1_prob_tables_conditioning.description: Read conditional probabilities from a two-way table. Choose the right denominator, test independence and recover unknown counts.

sections.title: What does each cell or total represent?
sections.label: Complete the table
sections.intro:
A two-way table classifies the same records in two ways. Row categories must not overlap each other, and neither must column categories. Each person appears in one interior cell. For two events A and B, the four cells represent both, A only, B only and neither. The row and column totals are marginal counts; the grand total is \(N\).

Complete missing cells using their row or column totals, then check that both sets of margins give the same \(N\). Counts are nonnegative integers. A probability table instead has nonnegative probability entries summing to one; those entries need not be integer counts.

blocks.html: Check what is selected uniformly. If each of the \(N>0\) people or items is equally likely, divide the event count by \(N\). The four cells are categories, not four equally likely elementary outcomes.

blocks.title: Reconstruct the four disjoint cells
blocks.prompt: One of \(50\) people is chosen uniformly at random. Of these people, \(22\) satisfy A, \(30\) satisfy B, and \(14\) satisfy both. Find the counts for A only, B only and neither, then find \(P(A\cup B)\).
blocks.hint: Subtract the intersection from each marginal count. Add the three different cells in the union; the remaining people belong to neither event.
blocks.solution:
1. \[n(A\cap B^{\prime})=22-14=8,\qquad n(A^{\prime}\cap B)=30-14=16.\]
  2. \[n(A^{\prime}\cap B^{\prime})=50-(14+8+16)=12.\]
  3. \[P(A\cup B)=\frac{14+8+16}{50}=\frac{19}{25}.\]

    The four counts sum to \(50\). Adding the marginal counts \(22+30\) without subtracting the overlap would count the \(14\) people in both twice.

sections.title: Which total becomes the conditional denominator?
sections.label: Choose the condition
sections.intro:
“Given B” restricts the space to B. Keep the count in both A and B as the numerator, and the whole B count as the denominator:

\[P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}=\frac{n(A\cap B)}{n(B)},\qquad n(B)>0.\]

Here \(n(E)\) means the number of records in event E. Reverse the condition and the denominator changes to \(n(A)\). For a complement or union condition, identify all its disjoint cells before adding their counts.

blocks.html:
Choose a student uniformly from the \(60\) shown. Let A mean club member and B mean bus traveller.

BB′Total
A121830
A′24630
Total362460
\[P(A\mid B)=\frac{12}{36}=\frac13,\qquad P(B\mid A)=\frac{12}{30}=\frac25.\]\[P(A\cap B)=\frac{12}{60}=\frac15.\]

Among the \(36\) bus travellers, \(12\) are club members. Among the \(30\) club members, \(12\) travel by bus.

The same intersection count gives different probabilities when the condition changes. Neither conditional uses the grand total.

An empty condition does not give probability zero. If the condition contains no possible records, its denominator is zero and the conditional probability is undefined. A zero numerator with a positive denominator does give zero. Also, \(P(A\mid B)\) and \(P(B\mid A)\) are not generally equal.

blocks.title: Choose the condition before the denominator
blocks.prompt:
One of the people in this table is chosen uniformly at random. Find the four conditional probabilities below.

\(B\)\(B^{\prime}\)Total
\(A\)\(9\)\(15\)\(24\)
\(A^{\prime}\)\(6\)\(10\)\(16\)
Total\(15\)\(25\)\(40\)
blocks.hint: The condition names the smaller space. For the last question, the condition contains the three union cells, and every member of A is inside that union.
blocks.solution:
1. \[P(A\mid B)=\frac{9}{15}=\frac{3}{5},\qquad P(B\mid A)=\frac{9}{24}=\frac{3}{8}.\]
  2. \[P(A^{\prime}\mid B^{\prime})=\frac{10}{25}=\frac{2}{5}.\]
  3. \[n(A\cup B)=9+15+6=30,\qquad P(A\mid A\cup B)=\frac{24}{30}=\frac{4}{5}.\]

    Each denominator counts the stated condition, not automatically the whole table.

sections.title: How can a table establish independence?
sections.label: Test independence
sections.intro:
Use one exact test:

\[P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B).\]

If \(P(B)>0\), the equivalent conditional test is \(P(A\mid B)=P(A)\). The product test remains valid even for a zero-probability event, when some conditional probabilities are undefined. Equal row sizes, equal-looking cells or mutual exclusivity are not independence tests.

blocks.html: For a fixed total \(N\), let the A count be \(r\), the B count be \(c\), and their overlap be \(x\). The four cells must be

\(B\)\(B^{\prime}\)Total
\(A\)\(x\)\(r-x\)\(r\)
\(A^{\prime}\)\(c-x\)\(N-r-c+x\)\(N-r\)
Total\(c\)\(N-c\)\(N\)

All cells must be nonnegative, giving the integer bounds

\[\max(0,r+c-N)\le x\le\min(r,c).\]

Independence requires

\[\frac{x}{N}=\frac{r}{N}\cdot\frac{c}{N}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=\frac{rc}{N}.\]

If this required overlap is not an integer, no exact count table with those margins is independent; do not round it to a person.

There is also a short check for a table whose four interior cells, in row order, are \(a,b,c,d\). With \(N=a+b+c+d>0\), the product test becomes

\[a(a+b+c+d)=(a+b)(a+c)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad ad=bc.\]

This is the same independence test after cancelling common terms, not a different assumption.

Keep \(60\) students, \(30\) club members and \(36\) bus travellers. Let \(k\) be the overlap.

BB′Total
A\(k\)\(30-k\)30
A′\(36-k\)\(k-6\)30
Total362460
\[k-6\ge0,\quad30-k\ge0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad6\le k\le30,\quad k\in\mathbb Z.\]\[\frac{k}{60}=\frac{30}{60}\cdot\frac{36}{60}=\frac3{10}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad k=18.\]\[P(A\mid B)=\frac{18}{36}=\frac12,\qquad P(B\mid A)=\frac{18}{30}=\frac35.\]

Keeping the margins fixed leaves one overlap count to choose. Every cell must stay nonnegative; independence selects one exact value.

Compare exact fractions or cross-multiplied integers. Rounded decimal equality can hide a difference. State the conclusion for the selection model described; an observed table alone does not prove that a wider population has independent characteristics.

blocks.title: Test independence with exact values
blocks.prompt:
One person is chosen uniformly from the following table. Calculate the joint probability and the product of the marginal probabilities, then decide whether A and B are independent. Separately, would an event with no members necessarily fail the product test?

\(B\)\(B^{\prime}\)Total
\(A\)\(6\)\(9\)\(15\)
\(A^{\prime}\)\(10\)\(15\)\(25\)
Total\(16\)\(24\)\(40\)

options.independent: Independent: the joint probability equals the product.
options.dependent: Dependent: the four cell counts are not all equal.

options.can: It satisfies the product test: its joint probability and its marginal product are both zero.
options.cannot: It cannot be independent because a conditional probability on it is undefined.

blocks.hint: Use the grand total for all three unconditional probabilities. Independence compares a joint probability with a product, not the four cell counts with each other.
blocks.solution:
1. \[P(A\cap B)=\frac{6}{40}=\frac{3}{20}.\]
  2. \[P(A)P(B)=\frac{15}{40}\cdot\frac{16}{40}=\frac{3}{20}.\]

    The exact equality proves independence for uniform selection from these records.

  3. If \(P(E)=0\), then \(P(E\cap B)=0=P(E)P(B)\). The product test remains meaningful, even though \(P(B\mid E)\) is undefined.

sections.title: How do I recover unknown cells or probabilities?
sections.label: Recover missing information
sections.intro:
Name the missing count, write the totals using it, then translate the given conditional or independence relation. Solve the equation and put each answer back into the original table. Every count must be an integer at least zero, the grand total must be positive, and every conditional denominator must be positive.

If probabilities describe an unknown finite population, multiplying each joint-cell probability by its proposed total must give an integer. Checking only the row and column totals can miss an impossible fractional cell. Retain every proposed total satisfying all the original constraints.

blocks.html:
Two reverse conditionals share one intersection:

\[P(A)P(B\mid A)=P(A\cap B)=P(B)P(A\mid B).\]

Start with a known marginal, find the intersection, then use the other conditional. If only two positive conditionals are given, they usually determine the ratio of the marginals, not a unique probability table.

Do not divide by a zero reverse conditional. If \(P(A\mid B)=0\), the intersection must be zero. A positive intersection makes the givens inconsistent. If the intersection is zero, that equation does not determine \(P(B)\); its original positive-denominator and cell-feasibility constraints still apply.

For example, if \(P(A)=a>0\) and both reverse conditionals are zero, the events are disjoint. A valid defined \(P(A\mid B)\) requires \(P(B)>0\), while the neither cell requires \(P(B)\le1-a\). Those constraints can leave several possibilities, rather than one answer.

blocks.title: Recover a marginal from the shared intersection
blocks.prompt: Events have \(P(A)=\frac{3}{10}\), \(P(B\mid A)=\frac{2}{3}\) and \(P(A\mid B)=\frac{1}{4}\). Find \(P(A\cap B)\), \(P(B)\) and the probability of neither event. Could the last given conditional instead be \(\frac{1}{10}\), keeping the other two givens unchanged?

options.no: No: it would require P(B) to be greater than one.
options.yes: Yes: every stated probability is between zero and one.

blocks.hint: The two conditional equations must describe the same intersection. Find its probability first, then divide by the positive reverse conditional.
blocks.solution:
1. \[P(A\cap B)=\frac{3}{10}\cdot\frac{2}{3}=\frac{1}{5}.\]
  2. \[P(B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(A\mid B)}=\frac{\frac{1}{5}}{\frac{1}{4}}=\frac{4}{5}.\]

  3. The other cells are A only \(=\frac{1}{10}\), B only \(=\frac{3}{5}\), and

    \[P(\text{neither})=1-\frac{3}{10}-\frac{4}{5}+\frac{1}{5}=\frac{1}{10}.\]

    All four cells are nonnegative and sum to one.

  4. With the proposed replacement conditional,

    \[P(B)=\frac{\frac{1}{5}}{\frac{1}{10}}=2,\]

    which is impossible. Valid-looking individual givens need not form a consistent table.

sections.title: Does the selection scheme change the table probabilities?
sections.label: Selection weights
sections.intro:
A count table describes the records. The selection rule assigns their probabilities. Uniform selection from all people gives a group a probability proportional to its size. Choosing equally between two nonempty groups, then uniformly within the chosen group, gives each group probability \(\frac{1}{2}\), even when their sizes differ.

For either scheme, calculate each group’s contribution as its selection probability multiplied by the required proportion within it. Add the contributions from the disjoint groups. For a reverse conditional, use the intersection and denominator from the same scheme.

blocks.html:
For two disjoint nonempty groups with sizes \(n_1,n_2\), let \(a_i\) be the number with A in group \(i\). If the group-selection probabilities are \(w_1,w_2\), with \(w_1+w_2=1\), then

\[P(A)=w_1\frac{a_1}{n_1}+w_2\frac{a_2}{n_2}.\]

Uniform selection from all individuals uses \(w_i=\frac{n_i}{n_1+n_2}\). Uniform selection between the groups uses \(w_1=w_2=\frac{1}{2}\).

Complete the model, not just the table. State who or what is selected, how it is selected, and whether repeated selections replace the item. With replacement, independent uniform selections can reuse the same proportions. Without replacement, update the relevant cell and total after the first actual selection. Independence of two characteristics on one person does not make different selections independent.

blocks.title: One table, two different selection schemes
blocks.prompt: Group East contains \(12\) people, \(9\) with a certificate. Group West contains \(36\) people, \(15\) with a certificate. The groups are disjoint. Scheme I chooses one person uniformly from all \(48\). Scheme II chooses either group with probability \(\frac{1}{2}\), then chooses a person uniformly within that group. For each scheme, find the probability of a certificate and the probability of East given a certificate.

fields.label: East given certificate under Scheme I
East given certificate under Scheme II

blocks.hint: Under Scheme I, every person has the same weight. Under Scheme II, first multiply each within-group proportion by the probability of choosing that group. Use the same scheme for both parts of each conditional.
blocks.solution:
1. \[P_{\mathrm{I}}(\text{certificate})=\frac{9+15}{48}=\frac{1}{2}.\]
  2. \[P_{\mathrm{II}}(\text{certificate})=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{9}{12}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{15}{36}=\frac{3}{8}+\frac{5}{24}=\frac{7}{12}.\]
  3. \[P_{\mathrm{I}}(\text{East}\mid\text{certificate})=\frac{9}{24}=\frac{3}{8}.\]
  4. \[P_{\mathrm{II}}(\text{East}\mid\text{certificate})=\frac{\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{9}{12}}{\frac{7}{12}}=\frac{9}{14}.\]

    Choosing equally between unequal groups gives different weights to their individual members.

glossary.definition: A table classifying the same records by a row category and a column category.
An interior cell containing records satisfying both its row and its column condition.
A row or column total, covering every cell in that category.
The total number \(N\) of records, counted once each.
The event treated as the restricted space in a conditional probability.
A conditional with the roles reversed, such as \(P(B\mid A)\) compared with \(P(A\mid B)\).
Events satisfying \(P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)\) in the specified probability model.
A table with valid nonnegative entries, consistent totals and any required integer counts or positive denominators.
Choosing so that every individual record has the same probability.
The complete rule assigning probabilities to the selected groups and individuals.
The probability assigned to a group or individual by the selection scheme.

examples.title: Fill the cells before adding event totals
examples.question:
There are \(60\) students. Let A mean “belongs to a club” and B mean “travels by bus”. The incomplete count table is below. Complete it, then find the probabilities of A or B, and neither, when one student is chosen uniformly.

\(B\)\(B^{\prime}\)Total
\(A\)\(12\)?\(30\)
\(A^{\prime}\)???
Total\(36\)?\(60\)
solution:
A only is \(30-12=18\). B only is \(36-12=24\). The final cell is \(60-12-18-24=6\).

\(B\)\(B^{\prime}\)Total
\(A\)\(12\)\(18\)\(30\)
\(A^{\prime}\)\(24\)\(6\)\(30\)
Total\(36\)\(24\)\(60\)

The union contains three different cells. Add the overlap only once:

\[P(A\cup B)=\frac{12+18+24}{60}=\frac{9}{10}.\]

\[P(A^{\prime}\cap B^{\prime})=\frac{6}{60}=\frac{1}{10}.\]

As a check, the union and neither form complementary events.

examples.title: Reverse the condition and change the denominator
examples.question:
One student is chosen uniformly from this club/bus table. Find \(P(A\mid B)\), \(P(B\mid A)\), \(P(A\mid B^{\prime})\), and \(P(A\mid A\cup B)\).

\(B\)\(B^{\prime}\)Total
\(A\)\(12\)\(18\)\(30\)
\(A^{\prime}\)\(24\)\(6\)\(30\)
Total\(36\)\(24\)\(60\)
solution:
Given B, only the \(36\) bus users remain in the space. Of these, \(12\) belong to the club:

\[P(A\mid B)=\frac{12}{36}=\frac{1}{3}.\]

Given A, use the \(30\) club members instead:

\[P(B\mid A)=\frac{12}{30}=\frac{2}{5}.\]

The intersection is unchanged, but the conditional probabilities differ.

\[P(A\mid B^{\prime})=\frac{18}{24}=\frac{3}{4}.\]

Both the numerator and denominator come from the not-B column.

The condition \(A\cup B\) contains \(54\) students, including all \(30\) club members:

\[P(A\mid A\cup B)=\frac{30}{54}=\frac{5}{9}.\]

examples.title: Find the overlap required for independence
examples.question: A student is chosen uniformly from \(60\) records. There are \(30\) club members, \(36\) bus users and \(12\) in both categories. Are club membership and bus use independent? Keeping the two category totals fixed, how many students would have to belong to both for independence?
solution:
\[P(A\cap B)=\frac{12}{60}=\frac{1}{5},\qquad P(A)P(B)=\frac{30}{60}\cdot\frac{36}{60}=\frac{3}{10}.\]

These exact values differ, so the events are dependent under this selection model.

If \(k\) is the required intersection count, independence needs

\[\frac{k}{60}=\frac{3}{10}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad k=18.\]

The resulting table is feasible:

\(B\)\(B^{\prime}\)Total
\(A\)\(18\)\(12\)\(30\)
\(A^{\prime}\)\(18\)\(12\)\(30\)
Total\(36\)\(24\)\(60\)

Its counts are nonnegative integers, and both original marginal totals are retained.

The conditional test agrees:

\[P(A\mid B)=\frac{18}{36}=\frac{1}{2}=P(A).\]

This test is valid because the B column has positive count.

examples.title: Solve a missing count and check the original table
examples.question:
One person is chosen uniformly from the following count table. Find the nonnegative integer \(k\) that makes A and B independent.

\(B\)\(B^{\prime}\)
\(A\)\(8\)\(12\)
\(A^{\prime}\)\(10\)\(k\)
solution:
The total is \(N=30+k>0\), the A count is \(20\), and the B count is \(18\). Therefore

\[\frac{8}{30+k}=\frac{20}{30+k}\cdot\frac{18}{30+k}.\]

Multiply by the positive square of the total:

\[8(30+k)=360\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 8k=120\quad\Longrightarrow\quad k=15.\]

The completed table is

\(B\)\(B^{\prime}\)Total
\(A\)\(8\)\(12\)\(20\)
\(A^{\prime}\)\(10\)\(15\)\(25\)
Total\(18\)\(27\)\(45\)

All counts are valid. Recheck the original probability equation:

\[\frac{8}{45}=\frac{20}{45}\cdot\frac{18}{45}.\]

examples.title: Recover a probability table from two conditionals
examples.question: Events satisfy \(P(A)=\frac{1}{3}\), \(P(B\mid A)=\frac{3}{5}\) and \(P(A\mid B)=\frac{2}{5}\). Find \(P(B)\) and all four joint regions.
solution:
Use the known marginal and its conditional to find the shared intersection:

\[P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B\mid A)=\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{3}{5}=\frac{1}{5}.\]

The reverse conditional is positive, so division is allowed:

\[P(B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(A\mid B)}=\frac{\frac{1}{5}}{\frac{2}{5}}=\frac{1}{2}.\]

Subtract the intersection from each marginal, then complete the total probability:

\[\begin{aligned}P(A\cap B^{\prime})&=\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{5}=\frac{2}{15},\\P(A^{\prime}\cap B)&=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{5}=\frac{3}{10},\\P(A^{\prime}\cap B^{\prime})&=1-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{5}=\frac{11}{30}.\end{aligned}\]

The four probabilities are nonnegative and sum to one. Both original conditionals check:

\[\frac{\frac{1}{5}}{\frac{1}{3}}=\frac{3}{5},\qquad \frac{\frac{1}{5}}{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{2}{5}.\]

examples.title: Compare uniform people with uniform groups
examples.question:
Two disjoint groups have the counts below. Scheme I chooses a person uniformly from all \(60\). Scheme II chooses North or South with probability \(\frac{1}{2}\), then a person uniformly within that group. Find the probability of a certificate under each scheme, and the probability of North given a certificate under each scheme.

GroupCertificateNo certificateTotal
North\(12\)\(8\)\(20\)
South\(10\)\(30\)\(40\)
Total\(22\)\(38\)\(60\)
solution:
Under uniform individual selection, the certificate count can be divided by the grand total:

\[P_{\mathrm{I}}(\text{certificate})=\frac{22}{60}=\frac{11}{30}.\]

Under equal group selection, use the two group branches:

\[P_{\mathrm{II}}(\text{certificate})=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{12}{20}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{10}{40}=\frac{3}{10}+\frac{1}{8}=\frac{17}{40}.\]

For Scheme I, the certificate holders are still equally likely:

\[P_{\mathrm{I}}(\text{North}\mid\text{certificate})=\frac{12}{22}=\frac{6}{11}.\]

For Scheme II, use its weighted intersection and its weighted certificate total:

\[P_{\mathrm{II}}(\text{North}\mid\text{certificate})=\frac{\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{12}{20}}{\frac{17}{40}}=\frac{12}{17}.\]

Under Scheme II, a particular North member has probability \(\frac{1}{40}\), while a particular South member has probability \(\frac{1}{80}\). The raw counts have not changed; the selection weights have.

extraPractice.title: Read the condition before choosing a total
extraPractice.prompt:
One item is selected uniformly from the following frequency table.

\(B\)\(B^{\prime}\)
\(A\)\(8\)\(4\)
\(A^{\prime}\)\(6\)\(12\)

Find \(P(A\mid B)\), \(P(B\mid A)\), and \(P(A\cap B)\). Decide whether A and B are independent under this selection model.

options.no: No: the intersection probability differs from the product of the marginals.
options.yes: Yes: any table with two separate classifications represents independent events.
options.unknown: The table cannot be used to test independence.

extraPractice.hint: The A row total is \(12\), the B column total is \(14\), and the grand total is \(30\). Select the total belonging to the event after the conditioning bar.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[P(A\mid B)=\frac{8}{14}=\frac{4}{7},\qquad P(B\mid A)=\frac{8}{12}=\frac{2}{3}.\]
  2. \[P(A\cap B)=\frac{8}{30}=\frac{4}{15}.\]
  3. \[P(A)P(B)=\frac{12}{30}\cdot\frac{14}{30}=\frac{14}{75},\qquad P(A\cap B)=\frac{20}{75}.\]

  4. The two values differ, so A and B are dependent for a uniformly selected item from this table.

extraPractice.title: Reconstruct the cells before restricting the table
extraPractice.prompt: Among \(72\) items, \(30\) have characteristic A, \(27\) have characteristic B, and \(12\) have both. Find the counts with A only, B only and neither. For a uniform selection, find the probability of exactly one characteristic and \(P(A\mid B^{\prime})\).
extraPractice.hint: Subtract the overlap from each marginal total. The neither count is what remains after adding the three disjoint inside regions.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[n(A\cap B^{\prime})=30-12=18,\qquad n(A^{\prime}\cap B)=27-12=15.\]
  2. \[n(A^{\prime}\cap B^{\prime})=72-(18+12+15)=27.\]

  3. The completed table is

    \(B\)\(B^{\prime}\)
    \(A\)\(12\)\(18\)
    \(A^{\prime}\)\(15\)\(27\)
  4. \[P(\text{exactly one})=\frac{18+15}{72}=\frac{11}{24}.\]

  5. The condition \(B^{\prime}\) contains \(72-27=45\) items, including \(18\) in A:

    \[P(A\mid B^{\prime})=\frac{18}{45}=\frac{2}{5}.\]

extraPractice.title: An unknown count must satisfy independence and integrality
extraPractice.prompt:
The following table contains counts, with \(n\) a non-negative integer.

\(B\)\(B^{\prime}\)
\(A\)\(5\)\(10\)
\(A^{\prime}\)\(9\)\(n\)

A uniformly selected item has independent classifications A and B. Find \(n\), \(P(A\cup B)\) and \(P(A\cap B)\). Separately, could the count table below describe independent classifications for a uniform selection?

\(B\)\(B^{\prime}\)
\(A\)\(4\)\(7\)
\(A^{\prime}\)\(5\)\(n\)

fields.label: Missing count in the first table
Union probability in the first table
Intersection probability in the first table
Can the separate table have an integer count n?

options.no: No: independence requires a non-integer count.
options.yes: Yes: round the algebraic result to the nearest whole count.
options.negative: Yes: a negative count can balance the table.

extraPractice.hint: For cells \(a,b,c,d\) in the displayed order, independence gives \(ad=bc\). Derive it from the joint and marginal probabilities if needed, then check the count restrictions.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[N=24+n,\qquad\frac{5}{24+n}=\frac{15}{24+n}\cdot\frac{14}{24+n}.\]
  2. \[5(24+n)=210\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n=18,\qquad N=42.\]
  3. \[P(A\cup B)=1-\frac{18}{42}=\frac{4}{7},\qquad P(A\cap B)=\frac{5}{42}.\]

  4. The completed first table has non-negative integer cells and its product test is satisfied. For the separate table, independence requires

    \[4n=7(5)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n=\frac{35}{4}.\]

    This is not an integer count, so no such frequency table exists. Rounding would destroy exact independence.

extraPractice.title: A zero marginal does not invalidate the product test
extraPractice.prompt:
One item is selected uniformly from this table.

\(B\)\(B^{\prime}\)
\(A\)\(0\)\(6\)
\(A^{\prime}\)\(0\)\(9\)

Decide whether A and B are independent. What is \(P(A\mid B)\)? Find \(P(B\mid A)\).

options.yes: Independent: the intersection and product of marginals are both zero.
options.no: Dependent: events with a zero marginal cannot be independent.
options.undefined: Independence is undefined for this table.
Undefined because the B column contains no items.
options.zero: Zero because the numerator is zero.

extraPractice.hint: The product definition of independence does not divide by a marginal. A conditional probability does, so check the particular denominator separately.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[P(A)=\frac{6}{15}=\frac{2}{5},\qquad P(B)=0,\qquad P(A\cap B)=0.\]
  2. \[P(A\cap B)=0=P(A)P(B).\]

    Thus the events are independent. B is empty in this finite uniform model.

  3. Conditioning on B would divide by zero, so \(P(A\mid B)\) is undefined. Conditioning on A is valid because six items belong to A:

    \[P(B\mid A)=\frac{0}{6}=0.\]

extraPractice.title: Use one intersection to connect two conditional directions
extraPractice.prompt:
Events satisfy \(P(A)=\frac{3}{8}\), \(P(B\mid A)=\frac{2}{3}\), and \(P(A\mid B)=\frac{1}{2}\). Find \(P(A\cap B)\), \(P(B)\), the probability of neither and the probability of exactly one.

Separately, suppose only \(P(A)=\frac{3}{8}\) and both defined conditionals \(P(B\mid A)=P(A\mid B)=0\) are known. Which conclusion about \(P(B)\) is justified?

options.range: No unique value: any \(0<P(B)\le\frac{5}{8}\) is compatible.

extraPractice.hint: Calculate the shared joint probability from A first. Dividing it by the positive reverse conditional then recovers B. In the separate zero case, do not divide zero by zero.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B\mid A)=\frac{3}{8}\cdot\frac{2}{3}=\frac{1}{4}.\]
  2. \[P(B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(A\mid B)}=\frac{\frac{1}{4}}{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{1}{2}.\]

  3. The four regions (both, A only, B only, neither) are

    \[\frac{1}{4},\quad\frac{1}{8},\quad\frac{1}{4},\quad\frac{3}{8}.\]

    All are non-negative and sum to one.

  4. \[P(\text{exactly one})=\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{4}=\frac{3}{8}.\]

  5. In the separate case, the intersection probability is zero. Because \(P(A\mid B)\) is stated to be defined, \(P(B)>0\). The remaining probability limits B to \(P(B)\le1-\frac{3}{8}=\frac{5}{8}\). Every value in that interval yields non-negative regions and both zero conditionals, so no unique marginal follows.

starters.title: Recover possible population counts from independent classifications
starters.question: An item is selected uniformly from a finite collection of \(N\) items, where \(50\le N\le120\) and \(N\) is an integer. Characteristics A and B are independent, with \(P(A)=\frac{3}{7}\) and \(P(B)=\frac{2}{5}\). Find every possible total \(N\). Additional information says fewer than \(20\) items have A only: select \(N\), then find the counts with both and with neither, and \(P(A\mid B^{\prime})\).
starters.hint: Both marginal counts must be integers. Then use independence to recover all four region proportions and apply the extra condition to A only.
starters.solution:
1. Since \(\frac{3N}{7}\) and \(\frac{2N}{5}\) are integer counts, N is divisible by both \(7\) and \(5\), hence by \(35\). Within the stated bounds this leaves \(N=70\) or \(N=105\).

  2. \[P(A\cap B)=\frac{3}{7}\cdot\frac{2}{5}=\frac{6}{35}.\]

    The proportions for both, A only, B only and neither are respectively

    \[\frac{6}{35},\quad\frac{9}{35},\quad\frac{8}{35},\quad\frac{12}{35}.\]

  3. Multiplying these by either candidate N gives non-negative integer counts. A only has count \(18\) for \(N=70\), or \(27\) for \(N=105\). Fewer than \(20\) therefore selects \(N=70\).

  4. The selected table is

    \(B\)\(B^{\prime}\)
    \(A\)\(12\)\(18\)
    \(A^{\prime}\)\(16\)\(24\)
  5. \[P(A\mid B^{\prime})=\frac{18}{18+24}=\frac{3}{7}.\]

    This equals \(P(A)\), as the original independence also implies independence from the complementary classification.

  • 1 mark: apply the strict A-only count condition.
  • 1 mark: recover the requested integer cell counts.
  • 1 mark: use the B-complement column total for the conditional probability.

starters.title: The selection scheme changes the probability weights
starters.question: East has \(20\) members, of whom \(4\) hold a certificate. West has \(30\) members, of whom \(18\) hold a certificate. The groups are disjoint. Scheme I selects one person uniformly from all \(50\) members. Scheme II selects East or West with probability \(\frac{1}{2}\) each, then selects one person uniformly within that group. For each scheme, find the probability of selecting a certificate holder and the probability that the selected person is from West given that they hold a certificate.
starters.hint: Scheme I gives equal probability to each person. Scheme II gives equal probability to each group, so people in the smaller group receive greater individual selection weight.
starters.solution:
1. In Scheme I, all \(50\) people are equally likely. With C meaning certificate and W meaning West,

    \[P_{\mathrm{I}}(C)=\frac{4+18}{50}=\frac{11}{25},\qquad P_{\mathrm{I}}(W\mid C)=\frac{18}{22}=\frac{9}{11}.\]

  2. In Scheme II, weight each within-group proportion by its group selection probability:

    \[P_{\mathrm{II}}(C)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{4}{20}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{18}{30}=\frac{1}{10}+\frac{3}{10}=\frac{2}{5}.\]
  3. \[P_{\mathrm{II}}(W\cap C)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{18}{30}=\frac{3}{10}.\]
  4. \[P_{\mathrm{II}}(W\mid C)=\frac{\frac{3}{10}}{\frac{2}{5}}=\frac{3}{4}.\]

  5. Scheme II gives a particular East member probability \(\frac{1}{40}\), but a particular West member probability \(\frac{1}{60}\). The raw grand-total fraction does not apply to that unequal-person-weight scheme.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: use the full count table for the uniform-person scheme.
  • 1 mark: restrict Scheme I to certificate holders.
  • 1 mark: use equal group weights for Scheme II.
  • 1 mark: calculate its certificate probability.
  • 1 mark: calculate the West-and-certificate joint probability under the same scheme.
  • 1 mark: divide by the correct Scheme II certificate probability.
  • 1 mark: explain why the two selection mechanisms give different individual weights.

revision.body:
Complete the counts, then choose the selection weights and denominator.

A uniform item selection starts from four disjoint cells

\(B\)\(B^{\prime}\)Total
\(A\)\(a\)\(b\)\(a+b\)
\(A^{\prime}\)\(c\)\(d\)\(c+d\)
Total\(a+c\)\(b+d\)\(N\)

Counts are nonnegative integers; \(N>0\). Count fractions require equally likely items.

\[P(A\cap B)=\frac{a}{N},\quad P(A\cup B)=\frac{a+b+c}{N}.\]

Exactly one has probability \(\frac{b+c}{N}\); neither has probability \(\frac{d}{N}\).

The event after the bar supplies the denominator

\[P(A\mid B)=\frac{a}{a+c},\qquad P(B\mid A)=\frac{a}{a+b}.\]

Use a positive denominator. Count all cells in the condition, then its required subset. Reversing a condition can change the answer.

Test independence and recover unknown entries

\[P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad ad=bc.\]

The product test allows zero marginals; conditioning on a zero marginal is undefined. Recovered counts must be valid integers.

Find \(j=P(A)P(B\mid A)\), then \(P(B)=\frac{j}{P(A\mid B)}\) if \(P(A\mid B)>0\).

Check all four probability regions. Two zero conditionals need not give a unique marginal; never divide by zero.

Choosing a group first changes individual weights

For two disjoint nonempty groups, choose group \(i\) with probability \(w_i\), then uniformly within it. Of its \(n_i\) items, \(a_i\) have A:

\[P(A)=w_1\frac{a_1}{n_1}+w_2\frac{a_2}{n_2}.\]

Uniform items: \(w_i=\frac{n_i}{n_1+n_2}\). Uniform groups: \(w_1=w_2=\frac{1}{2}\). Keep the same scheme when conditioning.

orig_9709_s1_prob_tree_mixtures.description: Use probability trees to combine routes to an event and work back to its source. Model repeated trials with shared or independently chosen sources.

sections.title: What does a branch probability actually mean?
sections.label: Reached branches
sections.intro:
A branch describes the next result given the history leading to its node. For example, the probability of passing a review after passing screening is a conditional probability. It is not automatically the overall chance of passing review.

Multiply the reached branch labels to obtain a complete route’s joint probability. The conditionals in this three-event formula require positive-probability histories: \(P(E_1)>0\) and \(P(E_1\cap E_2)>0\).

\[P(E_1\cap E_2\cap E_3)=P(E_1)P(E_2\mid E_1)P(E_3\mid E_1\cap E_2).\]

This rule does not require independence. Independence is the extra condition that allows a later conditional label to be replaced by its unconditional probability. A route with an unreachable prefix has probability zero; do not calculate an observed conditional on that zero-probability history.

blocks.html: Check each node and the complete tree. Outgoing branch probabilities at a reached node must be between zero and one and sum to one. Complete terminal routes are disjoint; their probabilities sum to one when all possible endings are included. End a route immediately when the process finishes, including a route with guaranteed acceptance.

blocks.title: Include the route that is accepted immediately
blocks.prompt: A request is accepted immediately with probability \(\frac{1}{4}\). Otherwise it is reviewed: its chance of passing review is \(\frac{2}{3}\). Given that it reaches the final check, its chance of passing that check is \(\frac{3}{4}\). A request that fails either check is rejected. Find the total acceptance probability and the probability of rejection specifically at the final check. Do these calculations require the stages to be independent?

fields.label: Probability of rejection at the final check

options.no: No: the later probabilities are already conditional on reaching their stages.
options.yes: Yes: probabilities can only be multiplied when stages are independent.

blocks.hint: The immediate route ends at acceptance. The other acceptance route must reach and pass both checks. Include the probability of reaching a stage before multiplying its conditional chance.
blocks.solution:
1. \[P(\text{accepted after checks})=\frac{3}{4}\cdot\frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{3}{4}=\frac{3}{8}.\]
  2. \[P(\text{accepted})=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{3}{8}=\frac{5}{8}.\]
  3. \[P(\text{final-check rejection})=\frac{3}{4}\cdot\frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{8}.\]

  4. Rejection at review has probability \(\frac{3}{4}\cdot\frac{1}{3}=\frac{1}{4}\). The terminal probabilities are therefore \(\frac{1}{4},\frac{3}{8},\frac{1}{8},\frac{1}{4}\), summing to one. No independence assumption was made: each later factor belongs to its reached history.

sections.title: How do I combine routes from different sources?
sections.label: Total probability
sections.intro:
Suppose exactly one of sources A and B is selected. Let their selection probabilities be \(w\) and \(1-w\), and their marked-item rates be \(a\) and \(b\). The marked event D can be reached through two disjoint routes:

\[P(D)=wa+(1-w)b.\]

This is total probability: add every source’s joint contribution to the same observation. Do not take an unweighted average unless the source weights justify it.

blocks.html:
Let D mean marked. Each row below multiplies its source chance by the chance of the final outcome within that source.

RouteJoint probability
\(A\cap D\)\(\frac25\cdot\frac15=\frac8{100}\)
\(A\cap D^{\prime}\)\(\frac25\cdot\frac45=\frac{32}{100}\)
\(B\cap D\)\(\frac35\cdot\frac1{20}=\frac3{100}\)
\(B\cap D^{\prime}\)\(\frac35\cdot\frac{19}{20}=\frac{57}{100}\)
\[P(D)=\frac8{100}+\frac3{100}=\frac{11}{100},\quad P(A\mid D)=\frac{\frac8{100}}{\frac{11}{100}}=\frac8{11}.\]

Multiply the source choice by the rate within that source. The marked branches contribute eight and three hundredths to the same observation.

For three disjoint sources covering all possibilities, use weights \(w_1+w_2+w_3=1\) and source rates \(a_1,a_2,a_3\):

\[P(D)=w_1a_1+w_2a_2+w_3a_3.\]

Each source contributes once. The same method works for a guaranteed-success source with rate one or a source that never succeeds with rate zero.

blocks.title: Add all three source contributions
blocks.prompt: Sources A, B and C are selected with probabilities \(\frac{1}{2}\), \(\frac{1}{3}\) and \(\frac{1}{6}\). Their marked-item rates are \(\frac{1}{4}\), \(\frac{1}{2}\) and \(\frac{3}{4}\), respectively. One source is selected, then one item is obtained from it. Find the probabilities of a marked and an unmarked item. Which source contributes the largest probability of a marked item?
blocks.hint: Multiply each source weight by its own marked rate. The source with the greatest weight or greatest rate need not make the largest joint contribution.
blocks.solution:
1. \[P(A\cap D)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{8},\quad P(B\cap D)=\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{6},\quad P(C\cap D)=\frac{1}{6}\cdot\frac{3}{4}=\frac{1}{8}.\]
  2. \[P(D)=\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{8}=\frac{5}{12},\qquad P(D^{\prime})=1-\frac{5}{12}=\frac{7}{12}.\]

  3. The largest joint contribution is \(\frac{1}{6}\), from B. Its source weight is not the largest, and its marked rate is not the largest; the product is what matters.

sections.title: How do I work backwards from an observed result?
sections.label: Reverse conditioning
sections.intro:
To find the source given an observation, first calculate all routes that could produce that observation. Their total becomes the denominator. The chosen source’s route is the numerator:

\[P(A\mid D)=\frac{P(A\cap D)}{P(D)}=\frac{wa}{wa+(1-w)b},\qquad P(D)>0.\]

For an unmarked observation, use the unmarked routes instead:

\[P(A\mid D^{\prime})=\frac{w(1-a)}{w(1-a)+(1-w)(1-b)},\qquad P(D^{\prime})>0.\]

blocks.html: The denominator includes every route to the observation. Neither the source weight nor a single branch rate is the required total. If the observation has probability zero, this conditional probability is undefined. A source with selection weight zero contributes no joint route weight; do not form a conditional on that unreachable source.

blocks.title: Reverse the source after either observation
blocks.prompt: Source A is selected with probability \(\frac{3}{4}\), and source B with probability \(\frac{1}{4}\). The marked-item rates are \(\frac{1}{10}\) for A and \(\frac{3}{5}\) for B. Let D mean that the selected item is marked. Find \(P(D)\), \(P(B\mid D)\), and \(P(A\mid D^{\prime})\).
blocks.hint: Calculate the two marked routes and the two unmarked routes separately. The observation after the vertical bar determines which route total is the denominator.
blocks.solution:
1. \[P(A\cap D)=\frac{3}{4}\cdot\frac{1}{10}=\frac{3}{40},\qquad P(B\cap D)=\frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{3}{5}=\frac{3}{20}.\]
  2. \[P(D)=\frac{3}{40}+\frac{3}{20}=\frac{9}{40},\qquad P(B\mid D)=\frac{\frac{3}{20}}{\frac{9}{40}}=\frac{2}{3}.\]
  3. \[P(A\cap D^{\prime})=\frac{3}{4}\cdot\frac{9}{10}=\frac{27}{40},\qquad P(D^{\prime})=\frac{31}{40}.\]
  4. \[P(A\mid D^{\prime})=\frac{\frac{27}{40}}{\frac{31}{40}}=\frac{27}{31}.\]

    Both denominators are positive. The source probabilities after an observation differ from the original selection weights.

sections.title: How do I recover an unknown probability or source weight?
sections.label: Unknown mixtures
sections.intro: Write the total-probability equation first, keeping the source weights and within-source rates separate. Solve it, then check every probability and complementary branch lies in \([0,1]\). Recheck the original total; if a reverse conditional is specified, its observation must also have positive probability.

blocks.html:
For a known overall probability \(m\),

\[m=wa+(1-w)b=b+w(a-b).\]

If \(a\ne b\), an unknown source weight is

\[w=\frac{m-b}{a-b}.\]

Require \(0\le w\le1\). Equivalently, \(m\) must lie between the two source rates. If \(a=b\), every valid \(w\) gives that same overall rate: matching data leave \(w\) undetermined; a different stated rate is impossible.

An unknown branch rate can be recovered only when its source has positive weight. For B,

\[b=\frac{m-wa}{1-w},\qquad w<1.\]

If B is never selected, \(m=a\) regardless of B’s rate. Consistent data then leave B’s rate free within \([0,1]\); inconsistent data have no solution.

When one parameter appears in several branches, solving may give several roots. Keep every valid root and its associated conditional answer until an extra condition selects one. If the question compares contributions to an observation, compare the joint weights \(wa\) and \((1-w)b\), not just the source weights.

blocks.title: Identify the mixing weight and its limits
blocks.prompt: The marked-item rates of sources A and B are \(\frac{2}{3}\) and \(\frac{1}{6}\). Source A is selected with probability \(w\). The overall marked probability is \(\frac{1}{3}\). Find \(w\). Could the same two rates produce an overall probability of \(\frac{3}{4}\)? Separately, if both rates were \(\frac{2}{5}\) and the overall rate were \(\frac{2}{5}\), would the overall rate identify \(w\)?

fields.label: Could the original rates produce an overall probability of three quarters?

options.no: No: it lies above both source rates.
options.yes: Yes: any probability between zero and one can be a mixture.

fields.label: What happens with two equal rates?

options.any: Every \(w\) with \(0\le w\le1\) gives the stated overall rate.

blocks.hint: Write the total as \(w\) times the A rate plus \(1-w\) times the B rate. A valid source weight must lie between zero and one.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\frac{2}{3}w+\frac{1}{6}(1-w)=\frac{1}{3}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2}w=\frac{1}{3}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad w=\frac{1}{3}.\]

  2. This is a valid weight, and substitution returns \(\frac{1}{3}\). The proposed overall rate \(\frac{3}{4}\) would instead give

    \[w=\frac{\frac{3}{4}-\frac{1}{6}}{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{7}{6}>1,\]

    so it is impossible.

  3. \[w\cdot\frac{2}{5}+(1-w)\cdot\frac{2}{5}=\frac{2}{5}\]

    for every valid \(w\). Equal source rates cannot identify the mixing weight from the overall rate alone.

sections.title: Are repeated outcomes independent if they share a source?
sections.label: Shared or fresh source
sections.intro:
There are two different experiments. In one, the source is selected once and used for both items. In the other, each item gets an independently selected source. State which experiment is being used before multiplying probabilities.

Suppose the item results are independent given their common source, with marked rates \(a,b\) and source-A weight \(w\). Let \(D_i\) mean item \(i\) is marked. With one shared source,

\[P(D_1\cap D_2)=wa^2+(1-w)b^2.\]

With independently reselected sources and independent item-generating experiments,

\[P(D_1\cap D_2)=\bigl(wa+(1-w)b\bigr)^2.\]

blocks.html:
Write \(D_1\) and \(D_2\) for the two mark events. Use the same source priors and within-source rates for the two models.

SourcePriorItem 1 mark rateItem 2 mark rate
A\(\frac{2}{5}\)\(\frac{1}{5}\)\(\frac{1}{5}\)
B\(\frac{3}{5}\)\(\frac{1}{20}\)\(\frac{1}{20}\)

One common source

\[P(D_1\cap D_2)=\frac25\left(\frac15\right)^2+\frac35\left(\frac1{20}\right)^2=\frac7{400}.\]\[P(D_2\mid D_1)=\frac{\frac7{400}}{\frac{11}{100}}=\frac7{44}.\]

Fresh independent source for each item

\[P(D_1\cap D_2)=\left(\frac{11}{100}\right)^2=\frac{121}{10000}.\]\[P(D_2\mid D_1)=P(D_2)=\frac{11}{100}.\]

Keeping one hidden source and choosing a new source for each item give different joint probabilities, even though each single-item marked probability is unchanged.

Conditional independence need not remain after the source is hidden. A first marked item can make the source with the larger marked rate more likely, changing the chance for the second item. A fixed source or equal source rates are special cases where the two formulas agree. If sampling within a source is without replacement, even conditional independence may fail: update the contents instead of automatically squaring a rate.

blocks.title: Keep or reselect the hidden source?
blocks.prompt: Sources A and B are selected with equal probability. Their marked-item rates are \(\frac{1}{4}\) and \(\frac{3}{4}\). In Scheme I, choose a source once and obtain two items whose marks are independent given that source. In Scheme II, choose a fresh source independently for each item, with the two item-generating experiments independent. Let \(D_i\) mean that item \(i\) is marked. Find the single-item marked probability, the probability that both are marked under each scheme, and \(P(D_2\mid D_1)\) under Scheme I.
blocks.hint: For one shared source, square each source rate before applying its source weight. For independent reselection, find the one-item overall rate first, then multiply that rate by itself.
blocks.solution:
1. \[P(D_i)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{3}{4}=\frac{1}{2}.\]
  2. \[P_{\mathrm{I}}(D_1\cap D_2)=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^2+\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^2=\frac{5}{16}.\]
  3. \[P_{\mathrm{II}}(D_1\cap D_2)=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2=\frac{1}{4}.\]
  4. \[P_{\mathrm{I}}(D_2\mid D_1)=\frac{\frac{5}{16}}{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{5}{8}.\]

    This differs from the unconditional \(\frac{1}{2}\), so the marks under Scheme I are not independent before the shared source is known.

blocks.html: In the model below, vary the source-A weight while keeping its marked rate at \(\frac{1}{5}\) and B’s at \(\frac{1}{20}\). Follow the joint routes and reverse conditional, then open the two-item comparison. Both marked and unmarked observations remain possible at either source-weight endpoint, so their reverse conditionals are defined there.

examples.title: Multiply the conditional labels on a three-stage route
examples.question: A request passes screening with probability \(\frac{3}{5}\). Given that it passes screening, it passes review with probability \(\frac{1}{2}\). Given that it passes both stages, it passes the final check with probability \(\frac{4}{5}\). It is rejected as soon as a stage fails. Find the acceptance probability and check that the complete terminal probabilities sum to one.
solution:
Let S, R and F mean passing screening, review and the final check. The acceptance route uses all three reached probabilities:

\[P(S\cap R\cap F)=\frac{3}{5}\cdot\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{4}{5}=\frac{6}{25}.\]

The first two rejection routes have weights

\[P(S^{\prime})=\frac{2}{5},\qquad P(S\cap R^{\prime})=\frac{3}{5}\cdot\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{10}.\]

Rejection at the final check requires reaching it first:

\[P(S\cap R\cap F^{\prime})=\frac{3}{5}\cdot\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{5}=\frac{3}{50}.\]

\[\frac{6}{25}+\frac{2}{5}+\frac{3}{10}+\frac{3}{50}=1.\]

Each route ends at its first rejection or final acceptance. The multiplication is valid because the later probabilities are conditional on their reached histories.

examples.title: Combine unequal source contributions
examples.question: Source A is selected with probability \(\frac{2}{5}\), and source B with probability \(\frac{3}{5}\). Their marked-item rates are \(\frac{1}{5}\) and \(\frac{1}{20}\). One source is selected and one item obtained from it. Find all four joint route probabilities and the total probability that the item is marked.
solution:
Let D mean “marked”. The A routes are

\[P(A\cap D)=\frac{2}{5}\cdot\frac{1}{5}=\frac{8}{100},\qquad P(A\cap D^{\prime})=\frac{2}{5}\cdot\frac{4}{5}=\frac{32}{100}.\]

The B routes are

\[P(B\cap D)=\frac{3}{5}\cdot\frac{1}{20}=\frac{3}{100},\qquad P(B\cap D^{\prime})=\frac{3}{5}\cdot\frac{19}{20}=\frac{57}{100}.\]
The unmarked total is \(\frac{89}{100}\). The four joint weights sum to one, and the two routes from A sum to \(\frac{2}{5}\), while the two from B sum to \(\frac{3}{5}\).

examples.title: Find the source after observing the item
examples.question: Source A has selection probability \(\frac{2}{5}\) and marked rate \(\frac{1}{5}\). Source B has selection probability \(\frac{3}{5}\) and marked rate \(\frac{1}{20}\). Given that the selected item is marked, find the probability that it came from A.
solution:
Keep both marked routes because either source can produce the observation:

\[P(A\cap D)=\frac{8}{100},\qquad P(B\cap D)=\frac{3}{100},\qquad P(D)=\frac{11}{100}.\]

The alternative source has conditional probability \(\frac{3}{11}\), and the two conditional source probabilities sum to one. The original source probability \(\frac{2}{5}\), the within-source rate \(\frac{1}{5}\), and the reverse conditional \(\frac{8}{11}\) answer different questions.

examples.title: Recover an unknown branch rate
examples.question: Source A is selected with probability \(\frac{1}{3}\) and has marked rate \(\frac{3}{5}\). Source B is selected otherwise and has unknown marked rate \(q\). The overall marked probability is \(\frac{2}{5}\). Find \(q\).
solution:
Use both disjoint routes:

\[\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{3}{5}+\frac{2}{3}q=\frac{2}{5}.\]
\[\frac{1}{5}+\frac{2}{3}q=\frac{2}{5}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad q=\frac{3}{10}.\]

The answer is between zero and one, its complementary B branch is \(\frac{7}{10}\), and substitution gives

\[\frac{1}{5}+\frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{3}{10}=\frac{2}{5}.\]

examples.title: Keep both valid probability branches
examples.question: Source A is selected with probability \(p\), otherwise B is selected. The marked rate is \(p\) in A and \(1-p\) in B. The total marked probability is \(\frac{13}{25}\). Find every valid \(p\) and its corresponding \(P(A\mid D)\). Then select the pair if A is chosen less often than B.
solution:
All weights and branch rates are valid exactly when \(0\le p\le1\). The two marked routes give

\[p^2+(1-p)^2=\frac{13}{25}.\]

\[25p^2-25p+6=(5p-2)(5p-3)=0.\]

Thus \(p=\frac{2}{5}\) or \(p=\frac{3}{5}\). Both lie in the allowed interval and both reproduce the stated positive marked probability.

\[P(A\mid D)=\frac{p^2}{\frac{13}{25}}.\]

Keep the answers paired:

\[\left(p,P(A\mid D)\right)=\left(\frac{2}{5},\frac{4}{13}\right)\quad\text{or}\quad\left(\frac{3}{5},\frac{9}{13}\right).\]
A is chosen less often than B when \(p<1-p\), or \(p<\frac{1}{2}\). This selects \(\left(\frac{2}{5},\frac{4}{13}\right)\).

examples.title: Compare a shared source with independent reselection
examples.question: Source A is selected with probability \(\frac{2}{5}\), source B with probability \(\frac{3}{5}\). Their marked rates are \(\frac{1}{5}\) and \(\frac{1}{20}\). Scheme I chooses the source once for two items, whose marks are independent given that source. Scheme II independently chooses a fresh source for each item, with independent item-generating experiments. Find the probability of two marked items under each scheme and the chance of a marked second item given a marked first item under Scheme I.
solution:
Under Scheme I, both items use the same source. Multiply the two conditional item rates before adding source routes:

\[P_{\mathrm{I}}(D_1\cap D_2)=\frac{2}{5}\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^2+\frac{3}{5}\left(\frac{1}{20}\right)^2=\frac{7}{400}.\]

Either single item has marked probability \(\frac{11}{100}\). Under Scheme II, the complete one-item experiments are independent:

\[P_{\mathrm{II}}(D_1\cap D_2)=\left(\frac{11}{100}\right)^2=\frac{121}{10000}.\]

For Scheme I, condition using its own joint weight:

\[P_{\mathrm{I}}(D_2\mid D_1)=\frac{\frac{7}{400}}{\frac{11}{100}}=\frac{7}{44}.\]

The first marked item makes source A more likely: its conditional source probability is \(\frac{8}{11}\). Weighting the second-item rates by these updated source probabilities confirms

\[\frac{8}{11}\cdot\frac{1}{5}+\frac{3}{11}\cdot\frac{1}{20}=\frac{7}{44}.\]

This exceeds \(\frac{11}{100}\), so conditional independence within a source has not produced independence when the shared source is unknown.

extraPractice.title: Include direct and reworked routes
extraPractice.prompt: An order uses process A with probability \(\frac{2}{5}\), and B otherwise. Its direct success probability is \(\frac{3}{4}\) on A and \(\frac{1}{2}\) on B. After a direct failure, exactly one rework is attempted: its conditional success probability is \(\frac{2}{3}\) on A and \(\frac{4}{5}\) on B. The order is accepted after either a direct or a rework success; otherwise it is rejected. Find the four requested probabilities.
extraPractice.hint: A rework path includes direct failure before rework success. Direct success and rework success are disjoint routes to acceptance.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[P(A\text{ and successful rework})=\frac{2}{5}\cdot\frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{2}{3}=\frac{1}{15}.\]
  2. \[P(\text{accepted}\mid A)=\frac{3}{4}+\frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{2}{3}=\frac{11}{12}.\]

  3. The four accepting routes, A direct, A rework, B direct and B rework, have probabilities

    \[\frac{3}{10},\quad\frac{1}{15},\quad\frac{3}{10},\quad\frac{6}{25}.\]
  4. \[P(\text{accepted})=\frac{3}{10}+\frac{1}{15}+\frac{3}{10}+\frac{6}{25}=\frac{68}{75}.\]
  5. \[P(\text{successful rework})=\frac{1}{15}+\frac{6}{25}=\frac{23}{75}.\]
  6. \[P(\text{successful rework}\mid\text{accepted})=\frac{\frac{23}{75}}{\frac{68}{75}}=\frac{23}{68}.\]

    The two rejecting routes have probabilities \(\frac{1}{30}\) and \(\frac{3}{50}\); together with acceptance they sum to one.

extraPractice.title: Keep all three sources in the denominator
extraPractice.prompt: One source is selected: A with probability \(\frac{1}{2}\), B with \(\frac{1}{3}\), and C with \(\frac{1}{6}\). Their respective success probabilities are \(\frac{1}{5}\), \(\frac{3}{5}\), and \(\frac{9}{10}\). Let S denote success. Find \(P(A\cap S)\), \(P(S)\), \(P(C\mid S)\), and \(P(A\mid S^{\prime})\).
extraPractice.hint: Weight each source-specific success chance by its source probability. For the final part, use failure probabilities in both the joint numerator and total denominator.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[P(A\cap S)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{5}=\frac{1}{10},\quad P(B\cap S)=\frac{1}{5},\quad P(C\cap S)=\frac{3}{20}.\]
  2. \[P(S)=\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{5}+\frac{3}{20}=\frac{9}{20}.\]
  3. \[P(C\mid S)=\frac{\frac{3}{20}}{\frac{9}{20}}=\frac{1}{3}.\]
  4. \[P(A\cap S^{\prime})=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{4}{5}=\frac{2}{5},\quad P(S^{\prime})=\frac{11}{20}.\]
  5. \[P(A\mid S^{\prime})=\frac{\frac{2}{5}}{\frac{11}{20}}=\frac{8}{11}.\]

extraPractice.title: A guaranteed branch and an impossible observation
extraPractice.prompt:
Route G is chosen with probability \(\frac{3}{10}\) and always succeeds. The other route succeeds with probability \(\frac{1}{7}\). Find \(P(S)\), \(P(G\mid S)\), and \(P(G\mid S^{\prime})\).

Separately, change the other route so that it also always succeeds. In this changed model, is \(P(G\mid S^{\prime})\) zero, one, or undefined?

options.zero: Zero, as in the original model.

extraPractice.hint: In the original model, failures occur only on the other route. In the changed model, check whether the conditioning event can occur at all.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[P(S)=\frac{3}{10}\cdot1+\frac{7}{10}\cdot\frac{1}{7}=\frac{2}{5}.\]
  2. \[P(G\mid S)=\frac{\frac{3}{10}}{\frac{2}{5}}=\frac{3}{4}.\]
  3. \[P(G\cap S^{\prime})=0,\quad P(S^{\prime})=\frac{3}{5},\quad P(G\mid S^{\prime})=0.\]

  4. When both routes always succeed, \(P(S^{\prime})=0\). Conditioning on failure is then undefined, not zero.

extraPractice.title: Recover a branch and respect the feasible range
extraPractice.prompt:
Route A is chosen with probability \(\frac{3}{7}\) and succeeds with probability \(\frac{5}{6}\). Route B is chosen otherwise and has success probability q. Overall success is \(\frac{13}{21}\). Find q and the largest possible overall success probability with these source weights and the same A success rate. Could the overall probability instead be \(\frac{19}{20}\)?

Separately, suppose A is always selected and overall success is \(\frac{5}{6}\). What can that observation determine about the success chance q of the unselected route B?

options.no: No: it exceeds the largest achievable total.
options.yes: Yes: it lies between zero and one.

options.any: The observation gives no further restriction: any \(0\le q\le1\) is compatible.
options.zero: It requires q to be zero.

extraPractice.hint: Use \(P(S)=\frac{3}{7}\cdot\frac{5}{6}+\frac{4}{7}q\). The largest total occurs at \(q=1\). A zero source weight removes its success chance from the mixture equation.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\frac{5}{14}+\frac{4}{7}q=\frac{13}{21}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{4}{7}q=\frac{11}{42}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad q=\frac{11}{24}.\]

  2. This is a valid probability and substitution recovers the original total. Since \(0\le q\le1\),

    \[\frac{5}{14}\le P(S)\le\frac{5}{14}+\frac{4}{7}=\frac{13}{14}.\]

  3. The proposed \(\frac{19}{20}\) is larger than \(\frac{13}{14}\), so it cannot arise from this mixture. Solving would require \(q=\frac{83}{80}>1\).

  4. In the separate zero-weight case, the total equation is \(P(S)=1\cdot\frac{5}{6}+0q=\frac{5}{6}\). It contains no information about q. Every probability \(0\le q\le1\) for the unselected route is compatible; a conditional probability given that zero-probability source is not defined by the observed mixture.

extraPractice.title: Recover the source weight, or recognise missing information
extraPractice.prompt:
Source A has success chance \(\frac{7}{8}\), source B has success chance \(\frac{1}{4}\), and the overall success chance is \(\frac{1}{2}\). Find the source-A weight w and \(P(A\mid S)\).

In a separate mixture, both source-specific success chances are \(\frac{1}{2}\). Does an overall chance of \(\frac{1}{2}\) determine a unique source weight? Could the overall chance in that separate mixture be \(\frac{3}{5}\)?

fields.label: Equal rates and total one half

options.any: No unique weight: any \(0\le w\le1\) is compatible.

options.impossible: Impossible: every weighted mixture retains the common success rate.

extraPractice.hint: Write the weighted sum before solving. If the two source rates agree, changing their weights cannot change the total.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\frac{7}{8}w+\frac{1}{4}(1-w)=\frac{1}{2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{5}{8}w=\frac{1}{4}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad w=\frac{2}{5}.\]
  2. \[P(A\cap S)=\frac{2}{5}\cdot\frac{7}{8}=\frac{7}{20},\quad P(A\mid S)=\frac{\frac{7}{20}}{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{7}{10}.\]

  3. For the separate equal-rate model,

    \[w\frac{1}{2}+(1-w)\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}\]

    for every valid weight. Thus the stated total gives no unique w; a total of \(\frac{3}{5}\) would be inconsistent.

starters.title: Retain both admissible roots before using extra information
starters.question:
Route A is selected with probability p, and route B otherwise, where \(0\le p\le1\). On route A the success chance is \(1-p\); on B it is \(\frac{1}{4}\). Overall success has probability \(\frac{3}{8}\). Find all possible values of p.

You are then told that the joint probability of A and success is strictly greater than the joint probability of B and success. Select the correct p, then find \(P(A\mid S)\) and \(P(B\mid S^{\prime})\) for this selected model.
starters.hint: Weight both success branches before solving the quadratic. Compare joint contributions, not the two source-specific success rates. Apply the strict extra inequality only after retaining all feasible roots.
starters.solution:
1. \[p(1-p)+(1-p)\frac{1}{4}=\frac{3}{8}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad8p^2-6p+1=0.\]
  2. \[(4p-1)(2p-1)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p=\frac{1}{4}\ \text{or}\ p=\frac{1}{2}.\]

    Both give valid branch probabilities and the specified total.

  3. At \(p=\frac{1}{4}\), both source-and-success contributions equal \(\frac{3}{16}\), so the strict inequality fails. At \(p=\frac{1}{2}\), the contributions are \(\frac{1}{4}\) and \(\frac{1}{8}\), so the inequality holds. Therefore choose \(p=\frac{1}{2}\).

  4. \[P(A\mid S)=\frac{\frac{1}{4}}{\frac{3}{8}}=\frac{2}{3}.\]
  5. \[P(B\cap S^{\prime})=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{3}{4}=\frac{3}{8},\quad P(S^{\prime})=\frac{5}{8}.\]
  6. \[P(B\mid S^{\prime})=\frac{\frac{3}{8}}{\frac{5}{8}}=\frac{3}{5}.\]

• 1 mark: form the weighted total-probability equation.
  • 1 mark: obtain and factor a correct quadratic.
  • 1 mark: retain and check both admissible roots.
  • 1 mark: compare joint contributions and select the root satisfying the strict extra inequality.
  • 1 mark: calculate A given success.
  • 1 mark: calculate the B-and-failure joint and total failure probability.
  • 1 mark: calculate B given failure using the selected model.

starters.title: A shared hidden source links two trials
starters.question:
One source is selected, A with probability \(\frac{2}{3}\) and B otherwise. Two trials then use that same source. Given the source, the trial results are independent, each with success probability \(\frac{3}{4}\) on A or \(\frac{1}{4}\) on B. Let \(S_1,S_2\) be success on the first and second trials.

Find \(P(S_1\cap S_2)\), decide whether the successes are independent before the source is known, and find \(P(S_2\mid S_1)\) and \(P(A\mid S_1\cap S_2)\). Finally, change the experiment: select a fresh source independently with the same weights before each trial, and generate the results independently within those choices. Find the new probability of two successes.
starters.hint: In the original experiment, multiply the two success chances within a source, then apply its weight once. In the changed experiment, each complete trial has a new independent source choice.
starters.solution:
1. \[P(S_1)=P(S_2)=\frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{3}{4}+\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{1}{4}=\frac{7}{12}.\]
  2. \[P(S_1\cap S_2)=\frac{2}{3}\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^2+\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^2=\frac{3}{8}+\frac{1}{48}=\frac{19}{48}.\]
  3. \[P(S_1)P(S_2)=\frac{49}{144}\ne\frac{57}{144}=P(S_1\cap S_2).\]

    The shared-source successes are dependent overall.

  4. \[P(S_2\mid S_1)=\frac{\frac{19}{48}}{\frac{7}{12}}=\frac{19}{28}.\]
  5. \[P(A\mid S_1\cap S_2)=\frac{\frac{2}{3}\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^2}{\frac{19}{48}}=\frac{18}{19}.\]

  6. After independent source reselection, each complete trial still has success chance \(\frac{7}{12}\), but now the two trials are independent:

    \[P(\text{two successes})=\left(\frac{7}{12}\right)^2=\frac{49}{144}.\]
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: obtain the common marginal success probability.
  • 1 mark: weight each same-source two-success path once.
  • 1 mark: calculate the shared-source joint probability.
  • 1 mark: compare it with the product and conclude dependence.
  • 1 mark: calculate the second-success conditional.
  • 1 mark: calculate the A-and-two-successes joint.
  • 1 mark: obtain the reverse source probability.
  • 1 mark: use independent complete trials for the changed experiment.

revision.body:
Label the history, weight every route, then restrict to the observed outcome.

Multiply along a path; add disjoint qualifying paths

For positive-probability histories:

\[P(E_1\cap E_2\cap E_3)=P(E_1)P(E_2\mid E_1)P(E_3\mid E_1\cap E_2).\]

Each branch uses its full preceding history. Reached-node branches sum to one, as do all complete terminal paths. Stop each path when the process ends.

Total probability and reverse conditioning

For two exhaustive disjoint sources A and B, let A have weight \(w\), with marked-item rates \(a,b\). Write \(m=P(D)\), where D means marked:

\[m=wa+(1-w)b,\qquad P(A\mid D)=\frac{wa}{m}\quad(m>0).\]

Include both marked routes in the denominator. For an unmarked item, \(P(A\mid D^{\prime})=\frac{w(1-a)}{1-m}\), requiring \(m<1\).

Include every source in the observation total. Conditioning on an impossible observation is undefined.

Recover an unknown, then check the original model

\[w=\frac{m-b}{a-b}\quad(a\ne b),\qquad b=\frac{m-wa}{1-w}\quad(w<1).\]

Every probability must lie in \([0,1]\), and \(\min(a,b)\le m\le\max(a,b)\). Check each candidate in the original model.

If \(a=b\), the total equals that rate and cannot identify w. A zero source weight leaves its unused rate undetermined. Keep all admissible quadratic roots until extra information selects one.

One shared source differs from a fresh source each time

Given one source, suppose two trials are independent with the same source-specific marked rate. Let \(D_i\) mean item \(i\) is marked. The probability both are marked is

\[J=wa^2+(1-w)b^2.\]

Compare \(J\) with \(m^2\) to test independence overall. If \(m>0\), then \(P(D_2\mid D_1)=\frac{J}{m}\). With a fresh independent source selection and independent result generation for each trial, the probability both are marked is \(m^2\).
